newsitem.title: USA: Fed seen notching rates up Tues - ex-Fed officials.
newsitem.headline: Fed seen notching rates up Tues - ex-Fed officials.

text.p: The Federal Reserve is expected to raise interest rates slightly at its policy meeting on Tuesday in a bid to ward off possible future inflationary pressures, two former Fed officials said.

"I think they should go," said Lee Hoskins, a former president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland. "It's the right thing to do in the sense of the uncertainy about potential inflation in the future."
The Fed's policy-setting body, the Federal Open Market Committee, will meet on March 25 to decide whether to change the course of monetary policy.

The Fed's target for the federal funds rate has been at 5.25 percent since January 1996, when the central bank trimmed short-term rates by 25 basis points. The Fed last hiked rates in February of 1995.
Hoskins said he would vote for a quarter point increase in the federal funds rate if he were still at the FOMC.
The former Cleveland Fed president added that he would also consider an increase in the discount rate, currently at 5.0 percent, by the same 25 basis points.

"If you want to make a strong statement, then you would increase the funds rate and then also move the discount rate," said Hoskins, who is currently the president and chief executive officer at Huntington BancShares Inc.
Hoskins said he based his analysis on current growth rates and the performance of the monetary aggregates over the last six months.
Richard Syron, a former president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Boston, also believed the Fed would likely tighten short-term interest rates at Tuesday's FOMC gathering.
"I've come around myself a little bit more to the school of ... favoring an increase. A minor increase of 25 basis points," said Syron, who is currently chairman of the American Stock Exchange.
Syron said current financial market levels were "way beyond" what economists thought just a few years ago would have incited inflationary pressures.
"At some point we will. We've been pushing the edge of the envelope for a while now," Syron said.
Current tightness in the U.S. labor market was also seen as an important factor driving a possible preemptive tightening of monetary policy.
Analysts said the current wage-moderating effect on inflation was likely to be temporary as continued strength in the labor market was likely to ease job insecurity at some point.
Syron said it was hard to know how long this effect could last, but he noted the Fed should be watchful.
"If I saw some straws in the wind, I'd be inclined to pay attention to them," he said.
The former Boston Fed head said there was one main constraint against an immediate tightening, though. "I think the big problem you have is the dollar. The dollar has been quite strong," Syron said.
However, a source close to the Fed said that at least one member of the Federal Reserve Board has expressed caution about raising interest rates at the March 25 meeting.

The source added that while some regional Fed presidents have sounded cautionary notes about the risk of possible future inflation, at least one member of the Board of Governors does not appear to share those concerns.
"I've felt no alarm on inflation from (this member of the board of governors)," the source, who recently spoke to the governor, told Reuters.

Some former Fed officials said they believe the outcome of the March 25 meeting is going to be a close call, and that Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan will be the key figure in deciding monetary policy at the March 25 meeting.

Former Fed vice chairman Preston Martin said he does not believe the Federal Reserve should increase short-term interest rates in March. "If I were there, I would not vote for an increase (in interest rates)," he said.
Martin said he believes Greenspan "will pass next Tuesday," adding that the odds favor a rate increase at the May 20 FOMC.
Martin said, however, he believes the composition of the FOMC -- which is down two governors -- appears to be a little more on the hawkish side.
"I think this will be a harder call and Greenspan will almost have to call it," said Martin, who is currently chairman of Home Vest Financial Services Inc.
Robert Holland, a former president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago, also said the vote of the chairman is key.
"The chairman only has one vote, but he has a lot of influence," Holland said.
While commenting on structural central bank issues, the former Chicago Fed chief declined to make predictions about what the Fed may do on March 25.
